generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, feedback in psychology arrives in more forms than a single grade: a mark, comments on your analysis, a completed rubric against the module criteria, a few spoken words after a seminar, even a comparison with a marked exemplar. Whatever form it takes, the useful step is the same: work out what it is asking you to do differently in the next report or essay, and treat that as the point of it rather than the verdict. Psychology deliberately pairs feedback with feedforward, so the comment is meant to carry into what you do next.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students get the same comment on a draft: You describe the study well, but you do not evaluate its methodology.

Tom reads the comment at face value, as a small complaint rather than an instruction, and misses the action it is asking for. Nothing changes in how he writes, so in the next assignment the same problem appears and the same comment comes back: the mistake has simply been repeated.

Amara works out the action behind the comment: it is asking for a judgement about the method, not more description. She plans the next piece around weighing the design, the sample and the measures against the claims, and writes to that. The next assignment evaluates the methodology, and the comment does not return.

Both read the same words. Only Amara read the action behind them and acted on it. That is what feedback is for in psychology: it tells you what to do differently, and acting on it is how your work improves from one report to the next.
generatedProse.summary: Feedback is the comments and insights that tell you how to improve, and in psychology it arrives in many forms, not just a mark. You can now recognise those forms, and, the skill that makes feedback worth having, work out the action a comment is really asking you to take. Reading the action behind the words, and feeding it forward into the next piece, is what turns feedback into better work.

check.body: A tutor writes on your psychology report: 'This is mostly description of the study; I would like to see more of your own evaluation of the method.' What is this comment asking you to do?

items.text: Weigh the study's method and evidence and show how convincing it is, rather than just reporting it.
Add more description to be thorough.
Change the study to an easier one.

feedback.correct: That's right. The comment asks for evaluation: weighing the method and evidence and judging how convincing it is, not more description or more words.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. The comment contrasts description with evaluation, so look for the option that asks you to judge, not to report.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The comment asks you to evaluate: to weigh the study's method and evidence and show how convincing it is. More words, more description or an easier study would each miss the action it is pointing to.
